examples.title: Chi-square test for a table
examples.prompt: Subjects at a military medical center were randomized to duct tape, cryotherapy or salicylic acid and checked for complete wart resolution after two months. Is there a difference in rates of wart resolution among the treatment groups? Use \(\alpha=0.05\), and do not isolate differences.

steps.say: This is a chi-square test because the outcome is a nominal count. The table is 2 by 3, with two outcomes in the rows and three treatments in the columns.
There is no difference in the rates of wart resolution among the duct tape, cryotherapy and salicylic acid groups.
Write the expected count, the chi-square sum and the degrees of freedom before any numbers go in.
Add across each row and down each column. Both sets of totals give the same grand total of 661 subjects.
Each expected count is its row total times its column total over 661. These six counts are what no treatment effect would look like.
The table is 2 by 3 and not 2 by 2, so no Yates correction is used. The six standardized gaps add up to 3.068.
There are 2 rows and 3 columns, so the test has 2 degrees of freedom.

The printed cutoff for 2 degrees of freedom at 0.05 is 5.991. Because 3.068 is below it, do not reject the null, so the resolution rates do not differ among the three treatments (P greater than 0.05).

examples.title: Pairwise chi-square with Holm from R output
examples.prompt: Heart attack patients got standard care (control) or one of three clot-dissolving treatments, and 30-day deaths were counted. R gave the Yates-corrected chi-square for all six pairs. Use the Holm correction with \(\alpha_T=0.05\) to find which treatments differ from the control.

steps.say: This is multiple pairwise chi-square tests with the Holm correction. Each pair of groups is its own 2 by 2 table of survived and died.
The question asks only which treatments differ from the control. So keep the three control comparisons and drop the three group versus group results.
There is no difference in 30-day mortality between the control and Group 1, AND none between the control and Group 2, AND none between the control and Group 3.
Every subtable is 2 by 2, so each comparison has 1 degree of freedom.
Control versus Group 3 is largest, then Group 1, then Group 2. The strongest result gets the tightest level.
The table has no 0.0167 column, so its cutoff sits between the printed 0.025 and 0.01 values on the 1 degree of freedom row.
18.234 clears even 6.635, and 9.4944 and 4.6895 clear their cutoffs too. No comparison fails, so all three nulls are rejected.
There is a difference in 30-day mortality between the control and Group 3, AND between the control and Group 1, AND between the control and Group 2. This whole statement holds with P less than 0.05.

examples.title: Goodness of fit
examples.prompt: Before a health campaign, 60% of graduating seniors reported no regular exercise, 25% sporadic exercise and 15% regular exercise. Four years later the seniors gave the counts below. Is there a difference in exercise behavior after the campaign?

steps.say: Multiply each old proportion by the 470 new seniors. These are the counts expected if nothing changed.
Each category gives one standardized gap, and the three gaps add up to 8.457.
There are 3 categories, so there are 2 degrees of freedom. Because 8.457 passes 7.378 but not 9.210, reject the null with P between 0.01 and 0.025, so exercise behavior has changed.
